    About IBC


         1.0 What is IBC?

          The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC)
                is a law which creates a consolidated framework
             that governs insolvency and bankruptcy
           proceedings for companies, partnership firms, and
             individuals.

          The IBC was enacted as a critical building block of
              India’s progression to a mature market economy.

                    It addresses the growing need for a comprehensive law that would be effective in
            resolving the insolvency of debtors, maximizing the value of assets available for
             creditors and easing the closure of unviable businesses.

        Four Pillars of IBC

       The institutional infrastructure under the IBC, 2016 rests on four pillars:

Timelines for Resolution

         On day one of the default, a creditor or borrower can approach NCLT to initiate
            insolvency proceedings.

         A case is admitted, NCLT appoints insolvency professional who is authorized to run a
          company for interim time till the case not solved. The professional’s task is to take
           necessary steps to revive the company.

            Within 180 days the lenders committee has to decide on a debt recast plan. Lenders
          would be given additional 90 days to arrive at a final plan.

                   If 66% of lenders agree, the committee would go ahead with debt restructuring
            otherwise after 180 days, the company’s assets will be liquidated.

          CIRP (including extensions & litigation) can be extended to 330 days.



        Resolution Process

         Default
     ↓
         Application to NCLT
     ↓
        Admission (within 14 days)
     ↓
        Moratorium (now the CIRP Timeline starts) (270/330 days)
     ↓
        IRP Appointed
     ↓
      CoC Formed
     ↓

Resolution Plans Invited
     ↓
      CoC Approval (66%)
     ↓
      NCLT Approval
     ↓
        Resolution

      OR

      No Resolution Plan
     ↓
         Liquidation



       PIRP

                    It introduced an alternate insolvency resolution process for Micro, Small and Medium
            Enterprises (MSMEs) with defaults up to Rs 1 crore called the Pre-packaged
           Insolvency Resolution Process (PIRP).

         A pre-pack is the resolution of the debt of a distressed company through an agreement
          between secured creditors and investors instead of a public bidding process.

           Pre-packs are largely aimed at providing MSMEs with an opportunity to restructure their
                liabilities and start with a clean slate while still providing adequate protections so that
            the system is not misused by firms to avoid making payments to creditors.

    IBC Amendment Bill 2026

          What: The Lok Sabha has passed the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment)
                 Bill, 2026 to speed up the insolvency resolution process and improve recovery from
            stressed companies.

             The bill has a total of 12 amendments, including 11 recommended by the Select
              Committee and one introduced by the government.

          1. Key changes introduced:

          The amendment sets strict timelines to make the insolvency process faster:

               Insolvency application timeline: Insolvency applications must now be accepted
                 within 14 days after a default is confirmed.

                Liquidation timeline: A timeline of 180 days has been set to complete the liquidation
              process (selling company assets), which can be extended by another 90 days if





10 years of IBC                                                                                                                        3

needed.

             The CIRP (Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process) was designed to be
              completed within 180 days, extendable up to 330 days in specified circumstances.

               Role of Committee of Creditors (CoC): The Committee of Creditors (CoC) will have
              a stronger role, meaning lenders will have more power in taking important decisions
               during insolvency resolution.

             Reducing delays and misuse: Since too many court cases were causing delays,
                the bill proposes steps to reduce unnecessary disputes. It also provides for
                penalties from ₹1 lakh to ₹2 crore for filing false insolvency cases.

          2. New insolvency resolution framework:

          The amendment introduces a creditor-initiated insolvency resolution process (CIIRP),
           which allows creditors to start the resolution process even outside the court system.
            This helps make the process faster and reduces legal delays. Can be initiated if atleast
         51% COC agrees.

                    It also includes concepts like:

               Debtor-in-possession model → The company’s existing management can continue
               running the business during resolution (with safeguards).

                Creditor-in-control approach → Creditors get more power in decision-making
               during the resolution process.

               Out-of-court settlements → Disputes can be settled without lengthy court
               procedures, saving time and cost.

          3. Group and cross-border insolvency:

            For the first time, the amendment introduces provisions for:

             Group insolvency → This Introduces a "voluntary group insolvency framework".
               This allows companies belonging to the same business group to be resolved
                together instead of separately, making the process more efficient.

              Cross-border insolvency → This helps creditors recover money from assets
                located in other countries when a stressed company operates internationally.

          These changes bring India’s insolvency system closer to global standards and make it
            easier to handle companies that operate in multiple countries.

          4. Protection of workers and stakeholders:

          The government has clarified that workers’ dues will get priority under the IBC
           framework. Their payments will be made before unsecured creditors and even before

some government dues. This ensures that while companies go through insolvency, the
            interests of employees are protected along with financial recovery.


    10 Years Achievements of IBC 2016

          What: Recently, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, completed 10 years
            since it came into force.

          As of March 2026, 1,419 cases had been successfully resolved through approved
             resolution plans, resulting in recoveries of more than ₹4 lakh crore for creditors.

          1. Performance of IBC in 10 Years:

           Over the last decade, the IBC has played an important role in resolving financial stress
          and reviving businesses.

                 Till March 2026, a total of 8,987 insolvency cases had been admitted under the IBC.

         One of the biggest achievements of the IBC has been the improvement in recovery for
             creditors.

            Resolution plans approved under the IBC have helped creditors recover more than ₹4
            lakh crore.

         On average, creditors recovered:

              About 95% of the fair value of the assets, and

              About 167% of the liquidation value, which is the amount they would have received
                         if the company had been liquidated.

       According to the RBI's Report on Trends and Progress of Banking in India 2024–25:

           Scheduled Commercial Banks recovered ₹1.04 lakh crore through various recovery
           channels during FY25.

           Out of this, nearly ₹54,000 crore (52.4%) was recovered through the IBC process
            alone.

        This shows that the IBC has become the most effective mechanism for recovering
        stressed loans and resolving bad assets in India.

          4. Improvement in Resolution Timelines

         One of the major achievements of the IBC has been reducing delays.

              Before IBC: Insolvency cases often took 6–8 years to conclude.





10 years of IBC                                                                                                                        5

After IBC, the average resolution time has reduced to around 2 years.

            This has helped preserve business value and improve recovery outcomes.

          5. Impact on NPAs and Credit Discipline

          The IBC has encouraged borrowers to repay their loans on time and has strengthened
             credit discipline in the economy.

             More than 30k cases were settled before being formally admitted under the IBC.

             These pre-admission settlements involved amounts worth nearly ₹14 lakh crore.

          The possibility of insolvency proceedings under the IBC encouraged many borrowers to
             clear their dues and settle disputes at an early stage.

          As a result, the banking sector has witnessed a significant improvement in asset quality.
          The Gross Non-Performing Asset (GNPA) ratio of banks declined from around 11.8% in
          2017 to 2.1% in September 2025.

            This shows that the IBC has played an important role in reducing bad loans and
           improving the overall health of the banking system.
